The contrast matrix needs to be full-rank.

  Matrix::rankMatrix(contrast.mat) # gives 3

You could change the 4th column to (1, -1, -1, 1)

  contrast.mat[,4] <- c(1, -1, -1, 1)
  Matrix::rankMatrix(contrast.mat) # now gives 4

karl

On 10/31/19 2:35 PM, John Lovell wrote:

> Hi Karl et al,
> I am working with a 4-way mapping population where parental genotypes [A,B,C,D] come from two subspecies:
> subspecies 1: [A,C]
> subspecies 2: [B,D]
>
> which produces four genotypes [AC,BC,AD,BD]:
> fixed subspecies 1: [AC]
> hybrids: [AD, BC]
> fixed subspecies 2: [BD]
>
> I want to use scan1coef to test three hypotheses with three separate contrasts:
> H0 #1: parent A is the same as parent B, contrast = c(-1,1,-1,1)
> H0 #2: parent C is the same as parent D, contrast = c(-1,-1,1,1)
> H0 #3: subspecies 1 is the same as subspecies 2, contrast = c(-1,0,0,1)
>
> So, I supply this contrast matrix to scan1coef:
>
> ```
> contrast.mat <-cbind(
>     mu = c(1, 1, 1, 1),
>     add1 = c(-1, 1, -1, 1),
>     add2 = c(-1, -1, 1, 1),
>     fixed = c(-1, 0, 0, 1))
> ```
>
> However, this matrix produces NAs for the fixed contrast. Is the issue the way that I am setting up the contrast matrix, or simply that I can't make this type of test simultaneously?
>
> Any help is much appreciated.
> Thanks,
> John
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
> Here is the code to replicate the issue:
>
> ```
> data(fake.4way)
> contrast.mat <-cbind(
>   mu = c(1, 1, 1, 1),
>   add1 = c(-1, 1, -1, 1),
>   add2 = c(-1, -1, 1, 1),
>   fixed = c(-1, 0, 0, 1))
> sex.matrix <- as.matrix(fake.4way$pheno[,"sex"])
> pheno.mat <- as.matrix(fake.4way$pheno[,"phenotype"])
>
> probs <- qtl2convert::probs_qtl_to_qtl2(
>   calc.genoprob(
>     subset(fake.4way, chr = 1),
>     step = 0))$probs
> rownames(pheno.mat) <- rownames(sex.matrix) <- 1:nind(fake.4way)
>
> s1coef.out <- scan1coef(
>   genoprobs = probs,
>   pheno = pheno.mat,
>   kinship = NULL,
>   addcovar = sex.matrix,
>   intcovar = sex.matrix,
>   se = TRUE,
>   contrasts = contrast.mat)
> ```
>

messages.subject: Corrections to CC variants SQLite database
messages.subject_clean: Corrections to CC variants SQLite database
messages.body_plain:
For those working with Collaborative Cross or Diversity Outbred mice and using the cc_variants.sqlite <https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.5280229.v2> database of polymorphisms in the CC founders, we've identified a couple of problems:
the ensembl_gene and consequence fields include at most one value, which is basically arbitrary in the case that a variant is in multiple genes or has multiple possible consequences
because of a bug in the script that created the database, only indels on chr 1-5 were included
I have a fix. The new database file is about 3.8 GB, and I'll try to upload it to figshare tomorrow.

The ensembl_gene field will have comma-separated ensembl IDs when a variant is in multiple genes, for example "ENSMUSG00000040354,ENSMUSG00000098057".

The consequence field will also have comma-separated values when there are multiple, and to distinguish which consequence corresponds to which gene, the values have the form "gene:consequence". So, for example: "ENSMUSG00000074657:synonymous_variant" or "ENSMUSG00000090036:upstream_gene_variant,ENSMUSG00000088687:downstream_gene_variant".

This is a bit more cumbersome to work with, but it provides more complete information.

karl

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl2-disc] plot phenotypes versus 3 SNP genotypes at particular SNP
messages.body_plain:
You could use the function predict_snpgeno() to collapse inferred diplotypes into SNP genotypes, based on the founders' SNP genotypes.
See the example in the help file for predict_snpgeno():
	file <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rqtl/" <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rqtl/>,
        	       "qtl2data/master/DOex/DOex.zip")
	DOex <- read_cross2(file)
	probs <- calc_genoprob(DOex, error_prob=0.002)

	# inferred genotypes
	m <- maxmarg(probs, minprob=0.5)

	# inferred SNP genotypes
	inferg <- predict_snpgeno(DOex, m)

Alternatively, you can collapse the genotype probabilities to SNP probabilities using genoprob_to_snpprob() and then use maxmarg() with those probabilities.

	# convert diplotype probabilities to SNP genotype probabilities
	snp_probs <- genoprob_to_snpprob(probs, DOex)

	# get inferred SNP genotypes at a particular position
	inferg <- maxmarg(snp_probs, DOex$pmap, chr=2, pos=96.842, return_char=TRUE)

	# plot phenotype vs inferred SNP genotype
	plot_pxg(inferg, DOex$pheno)

karl

messages.subject: Re: Phenotype distribution
messages.body_plain:
It would be helpful if you said more about the nature of your phenotype distribution.

Generally, your options are (a) transform (for example square-root or log), (b) convert to ranks or normal quantiles (such as with the R/qtl1 function nqrank()), or (c) change the method of analysis (such as using a generalized linear model). QTL mapping is basically just linear regression, and so whatever you might do in linear regression to deal with non-normal traits could also be used in QTL mapping.

The output of calc_genoprob() is a list of 3d arrays of genotype probabilities. You can use those directly in whatever sort of analysis you want.

karl

>
> I'm working on a tutorial on data diagnostics in multiparent populations such as the DO, but it's been slow going and probably won't be done until late spring.
>
> My basic approach is
>
> 1. Verify mouse sex, principally be looking at probe intensities for SNPs on X and Y chromosome. The proportion of heterozygous genotypes on the X is also informative.
>
> 2. Look for sample duplicates, by counting the proportion of SNPs with matching genotypes for each pair of samples.
>
> 3. Look at the proportion of missing genotypes for each sample, as a way to identify poorly behaved samples. The distribution of SNP array intensities also seems a useful guide.
>
> 4. Look at estimated counts of crossovers across the genome.
>
> But you were interested particularly in allele frequencies across the genome. The function calc_geno_freq() is useful for this. You can use either the results of calc_genoprob (with all 36 genotypes), or the allele dosages from genoprob_to_alleleprob().
>
> If you want to look at the genotype reconstructions for individuals, you can use
>
>    plot_genoprob() - heatmap of genotype probabilities for a single individual on a single chromosome
>    plot_onegeno() - genome-wide inferred genotypes for a single individual, after first using maxmarg()
>                     to infer genotypes and guess_phase() to guess the haplotypes
>
> I paste some example code, below.
>
> karl
>
> --------
>
>

> DOex <- read_cross2(file)
>
> # genoprobs
> pr <- calc_genoprob(DOex, error_prob=0.002)
>
> # allele probs
> apr <- genoprob_to_alleleprob(pr)
>
> # histograms of allele frequencies across individuals
> af_ind <- calc_geno_freq(apr, "individual")
> par(mfrow=c(4,2))
> for(i in 1:8) hist(af[,i], main=colnames(af)[i], breaks=30)
>
> # plots of allele frequencies across the genome
> af_mar <- calc_geno_freq(apr, "marker", omit_x=FALSE)
> plot_coefCC(af_mar, DOex$pmap, ylim=c(0, max(af_mar)), ylab="Allele frequency")
>
> # heatmap of genotype probabilities for a single individual on one chromosome
> plot_genoprob(pr, DOex$pmap, chr="2", ind=1, threshold=1/8)
>
> # plot of a single individual's inferred genotypes
> ### first infer genotypes
> m <- maxmarg(pr)
> ### then guess phase (so we can look at the two haplotypes
> v <- guess_phase(DOex, m)
> ### now the plot
> plot_onegeno(v, DOex$pmap, ind=1) # a male
> plot_onegeno(v, DOex$pmap, ind=53) # a female
>

> >> >>     On Thursday, February 22, 2018 at 10:22:52 AM UTC-6, Karl Broman
> >> >>     wrote:
> >> >>
> >> >>
> >> >>
> >> >>         > Is there a way to summarize/visualize the basic haplotype
> >> >>         reconstructions for all mice.  For example, it would be nice
> >> >>         to see an analysis/graph of some sort that summarizes all of
> >> >>         those haplotype reconstructions to show what founder
> >> >>         contributions exist across the entire genome in a DO cohort
> >> >>         (basically something to show that equal founder contribution
> >> >>         was maintained in the xth generation DO cohort that was used).
> >> >>
> >> >>         I'm working on a tutorial on data diagnostics in multiparent
> >> >>         populations such as the DO, but it's been slow going and
> >> >>         probably won't be done until late spring.
> >> >>
> >> >>         My basic approach is
> >> >>
> >> >>         1. Verify mouse sex, principally be looking at probe
> >> >>         intensities for SNPs on X and Y chromosome. The proportion of
> >> >>         heterozygous genotypes on the X is also informative.
> >> >>
> >> >>         2. Look for sample duplicates, by counting the proportion of
> >> >>         SNPs with matching genotypes for each pair of samples.
> >> >>
> >> >>         3. Look at the proportion of missing genotypes for each
> >> >>         sample, as a way to identify poorly behaved samples. The
> >> >>         distribution of SNP array intensities also seems a useful guide.
> >> >>
> >> >>         4. Look at estimated counts of crossovers across the genome.
> >> >>
> >> >>         But you were interested particularly in allele frequencies
> >> >>         across the genome. The function calc_geno_freq() is useful
> >> >>         for this. You can use either the results of calc_genoprob
> >> >>         (with all 36 genotypes), or the allele dosages from
> >> >>         genoprob_to_alleleprob().
> >> >>
> >> >>         If you want to look at the genotype reconstructions for
> >> >>         individuals, you can use
> >> >>
> >> >>            plot_genoprob() - heatmap of genotype probabilities for a
> >> >>         single individual on a single chromosome
> >> >>            plot_onegeno() - genome-wide inferred genotypes for a
> >> >>         single individual, after first using maxmarg()
> >> >>                             to infer genotypes and guess_phase() to
> >> >>         guess the haplotypes
> >> >>
> >> >>         I paste some example code, below.
> >> >>
> >> >>         karl
> >> >>
> >> >>         --------
> >> >>
> >> >>
> >> >>         # Example with the DOex data
> >> >>         (https://github.com/rqtl/qtl2data/tree/master/DOex
> >> >>         <https://github.com/rqtl/qtl2data/tree/master/DOex>)
> >> >>
> >> >>         library(qtl2)
> >> >>         file <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rqtl/
> >> >>         <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rqtl/>",
> >> >>                        "qtl2data/master/DOex/DOex.zip")
> >> >>         DOex <- read_cross2(file)
> >> >>
> >> >>         # genoprobs
> >> >>         pr <- calc_genoprob(DOex, error_prob=0.002)
> >> >>
> >> >>         # allele probs
> >> >>         apr <- genoprob_to_alleleprob(pr)
> >> >>
> >> >>         # histograms of allele frequencies across individuals
> >> >>         af_ind <- calc_geno_freq(apr, "individual")
> >> >>         par(mfrow=c(4,2))
> >> >>         for(i in 1:8) hist(af[,i], main=colnames(af)[i], breaks=30)
> >> >>
> >> >>         # plots of allele frequencies across the genome
> >> >>         af_mar <- calc_geno_freq(apr, "marker", omit_x=FALSE)
> >> >>         plot_coefCC(af_mar, DOex$pmap, ylim=c(0, max(af_mar)),
> >> >>         ylab="Allele frequency")
> >> >>
> >> >>         # heatmap of genotype probabilities for a single individual
> >> >>         on one chromosome
> >> >>         plot_genoprob(pr, DOex$pmap, chr="2", ind=1, threshold=1/8)
> >> >>
> >> >>         # plot of a single individual's inferred genotypes
> >> >>         ### first infer genotypes
> >> >>         m <- maxmarg(pr)
> >> >>         ### then guess phase (so we can look at the two haplotypes
> >> >>         v <- guess_phase(DOex, m)
> >> >>         ### now the plot
> >> >>         plot_onegeno(v, DOex$pmap, ind=1) # a male
> >> >>         plot_onegeno(v, DOex$pmap, ind=53) # a female
> >> >>
